beats.intro: Chapter eight, lesson 3. Free energy, stability and equilibrium. [[ball]]A ball on a high ledge is unstable. Give it a nudge and it rolls down, and it never rolls back up on its own. [[cells]]Chemical reactions inside a cell behave the same way. [[strip]]Here is our pathway strip again. [[drop]]Today we light the drop in energy along it. Each arrow is a step downhill, and free energy tells us whether a step will run by itself.
beats.formula: [[free]]Free energy is the energy of a system that can do work, when temperature and pressure are uniform, as they are in a living cell. Biologists write its change as delta G. [[eq]]Delta G equals delta H, minus T times delta S. Delta H is the change in total energy, called enthalpy. Delta S is the change in entropy, the disorder. And T is the temperature, in Kelvin. [[kelvin]]Body temperature, thirty-seven degrees Celsius, is about three hundred ten Kelvin. [[neg]]Here is the rule. Only a process with a negative delta G is spontaneous. And spontaneous processes can be harnessed to do work. [[ex]]A worked example, with made-up numbers. Suppose delta H is minus five kilocalories per mole, and T times delta S is plus three. Then delta G is minus five, minus three, which is minus eight. Negative, so the reaction runs by itself. [[more]]Notice that a bigger rise in disorder makes delta G more negative.
beats.stable: [[inst]]Free energy is also a measure of a system's instability, its tendency to change to a more stable state. [[down]]During a spontaneous change, free energy decreases and stability increases. Like the ball, the system settles lower. [[equil]]Equilibrium is the state of maximum stability. There the free energy is as low as it can go, and delta G equals zero. [[nowork]]So a process can do work only while it is moving toward equilibrium. A ball at the bottom of the hill can do nothing.
beats.q1: Quick check. Is each change spontaneous, or not?
beats.diagram: [[exer]]Now the two kinds of reaction. In an exergonic reaction, the reactants start high and the products end lower. Free energy is released, delta G is less than zero, and the reaction is spontaneous. [[endo]]In an endergonic reaction, the products sit higher than the reactants. The reaction absorbs free energy from its surroundings, delta G is greater than zero, and it is nonspontaneous. It will not go unless energy is put in. [[rev]]So exergonic gives energy out, and endergonic takes energy in. [[glu]]Breaking down glucose in cellular respiration is exergonic. Building a protein is endergonic.
beats.q2: Quick check. Which reaction needs an input of energy?
beats.cells: [[closed]]If reactions run in a system with nothing flowing in or out, they eventually reach equilibrium, and then they do no work. [[open]]A cell is different. A cell is an open system, with a constant flow of materials in and out. [[never]]So a feature of life is that metabolism is never at equilibrium. [[cat]]A catabolic pathway releases free energy in a series of reactions, so the cell always has a drop to run on.
beats.hydro: Three water systems show this. [[a]]In the first, water runs from the high tank to the low one through a turbine, and lights a bulb. When the two levels match, delta G is zero, and the bulb goes out. [[b]]In the second, a tap keeps filling the top tank, and the water drains away at the bottom. It never levels, so the bulb keeps shining. That is an open system. [[c]]In the third, the water falls through several steps, each with its own turbine. Every step has a negative delta G. That is a metabolic pathway: a series of downhill steps, each one able to do work.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[s1]]Delta G equals delta H minus T delta S, and a negative delta G means spontaneous. [[s2]]Free energy falls and stability rises, until equilibrium, where delta G is zero and no work is done. [[s3]]Exergonic reactions release energy. Endergonic reactions absorb it. [[s4]]Cells are open systems, so they never reach equilibrium. Now try the practice.
